'name' is interpolated directly into a PowerShell path glob (it cannot be single-quoted because it sits next to the $SitecoreDataFolder variable and a * wildcard), but the zod schema restricts it to /^[A-Za-z0-9._*-]*$/ -- fully anchored, no '/', ';', '|', '$', backtick or quote characters possible -- verified in src/tools/powershell/composite/logging/get-logs.ts. tail/skip/first-like numeric params are zod-typed numbers, not strings, so they cannot carry script syntax either.

'saveTo' (the only local-filesystem write this tool does) goes through resolveLocalMediaPath, which confines it to MEDIA_LOCAL_FILE_ROOT (path.relative()-based containment check) when set, and refuses local paths entirely over the HTTP transport when MEDIA_LOCAL_FILE_ROOT is unset -- verified in src/tools/powershell/media/local-files.ts and media-download.ts. The media item 'path' only ever reaches Sitecore's own media service URL (percent-encoded per path segment in media-service.ts).

'command'/'category'/'search' are matched against an in-memory index built once from a fixed, vendored directory list (DOCUMENTATION_CATEGORIES); findCommand() does a case-insensitive equality match against doc.name in that index and only then reads doc.file, a path the index itself computed -- no caller string is ever concatenated into a filesystem path (src/tools/powershell/documentation-index.ts).

excerpt: addresses = await lookup(url.hostname, { all: true }); ... const blocked = addresses.filter(...)
sink: server-side fetch() of a caller-supplied URL, after a one-time DNS-based private-IP check
guard: bypassable: DNS-rebinding -- attacker's nameserver returns a public IP for the check-time lookup() and a private/link-local IP for the later fetch()-time resolution
why: sourceUrl is fetched by the server itself. assertFetchableSourceUrl (src/tools/powershell/media/local-files.ts) blocks private/loopback/link-local addresses by calling dns.lookup() on the hostname and rejecting if any resolved address is private -- a real allow-list. But the actual request is then made with Node's global fetch() (utils.ts fetchWithTimeout), which performs its OWN independent DNS resolution at connect time. Because the check and the connect are two separate DNS lookups, an attacker who controls authoritative DNS for the sourceUrl hostname can answer the first lookup (the check) with a public IP and the second lookup (the actual fetch/connect, moments later) with 169.254.169.254 or another RFC1918 address -- classic DNS-rebinding TOCTOU. The per-redirect re-validation in fetchSourceUrl closes the redirect-based bypass but does nothing for this one, since it re-runs the same check-then-fetch pattern. Concrete bypass: host a domain whose authoritative nameserver returns 93.184.216.34 (public) on the first A query and 169.254.169.254 on the second/subsequent A query (TTL=0/1), then pass http://that-domain/ as sourceUrl.
contract: Source is exactly one of sourceUrl (fetched by this server -- use this to import from a live site), filePath ..., or content (base64).

sink: unescaped path segment in an Item Service REST GET URL (RestfulItemServiceClient.getItemById)
why: 'id' is a plain z.string() with no GUID/format restriction, and is concatenated unescaped directly into the Item Service REST URL path (getItemById, src/tools/item-service/client.ts line 149), unlike the sibling getItemByPath()/createItem() methods in the same file which correctly wrap their path input in encodeURIComponent (lines 243 and 286). Node's fetch() constructs a WHATWG URL from this string, which performs RFC-3986 dot-segment normalization on the path component: a value such as '../../users' collapses one or more '/sitecore/api/ssc/item/' segments away and can redirect the authenticated request (same session cookie) to a different path under the same Item Service host -- reaching an endpoint this tool's own declared 'by ID' contract does not intend to expose, and potentially bypassing any path-scoped access control (e.g. a reverse proxy/WAF rule) that assumes traffic only ever hits /item/<opaque-id>. Impact beyond that (which other same-host endpoints exist and what they expose) depends on the specific Sitecore/Item-Service deployment, which cannot be confirmed from this repo alone.

contract: Delete a Sitecore item by its ID.

sink: unescaped path segment in an Item Service REST GET URL (RestfulItemServiceClient.getItemChildren)
why: 'id' is a plain z.string() with no GUID/format restriction, and is concatenated unescaped directly into the Item Service REST URL path (getItemChildren, src/tools/item-service/client.ts line 195), unlike the sibling getItemByPath()/createItem() methods in the same file which correctly wrap their path input in encodeURIComponent (lines 243 and 286). Node's fetch() constructs a WHATWG URL from this string, which performs RFC-3986 dot-segment normalization on the path component: a value such as '../../users' collapses one or more '/sitecore/api/ssc/item/' segments away and can redirect the authenticated request (same session cookie) to a different path under the same Item Service host -- reaching an endpoint this tool's own declared 'by ID' contract does not intend to expose, and potentially bypassing any path-scoped access control (e.g. a reverse proxy/WAF rule) that assumes traffic only ever hits /item/<opaque-id>. Impact beyond that (which other same-host endpoints exist and what they expose) depends on the specific Sitecore/Item-Service deployment, which cannot be confirmed from this repo alone.
contract: Get the direct children of a Sitecore item by its ID, with all their fields.

excerpt: const children = await client.getItemChildren(idToProcess, options) as any;
sink: root 'id' flows unescaped into the same getItemChildren() REST GET URL as item-service-get-item-children
why: This tool's caller-supplied root 'id' (src/tools/item-service/logic/composite/get-item-descendants.ts) is passed straight into RestfulItemServiceClient.getItemChildren, which concatenates it unescaped into the REST URL path (client.ts line 195) -- the same missing-encodeURIComponent gap as item-service-get-item-children. Only the root id is caller-controlled; subsequent queue entries come from Sitecore's own ItemID field values, so the injection surface is limited to the first request of the traversal.
contract: Gets every descendant of a Sitecore item by ID, with all their fields.

param: GRAPHQL_HEADERS (server config, reflected verbatim in the tool's own output)
sink: server config value returned unmasked in the 'config' tool's CallToolResult / config://main resource
guard: partial: redactConfig masks every credential field it enumerates (apiKey, both passwords, authoring token/secret, authorizationHeader) but omits graphQL.headers, an operator-supplied arbitrary header map that is exactly where a custom secret header would live
why: redactConfig() (src/config.ts, ~line 229) masks graphQL.apiKey, itemService.password, powershell.password, authoring.token, authoring.clientSecret and authorizationHeader before the 'config' tool/'config://main' resource return the config -- but it does not mask 'graphQL.headers', a caller-configurable map populated from the GRAPHQL_HEADERS env var (parseGraphQLHeaders, config.ts line 143) that operators use for exactly the kind of value redactConfig otherwise exists to hide -- a custom Authorization/X-Api-Key header for a gateway in front of the GraphQL Edge endpoint. If an operator sets such a header, its value is returned verbatim by this read-only tool to anyone who can call it, which over TRANSPORT=streamable-http (AUTHORIZATION_HEADER empty by default per this repo's own AGENTS.md) is anyone who can reach the port. This depends on whether an operator actually put a secret in GRAPHQL_HEADERS, which cannot be confirmed statically.
contract: Prints the configuration of the Sitecore MCP server. Secrets (passwords, the GraphQL API key, the authorization header) are redacted.
